svg.title: The size of the flooding domain as a quantitative constraint on link-state design
svg.desc: A curve rising steeply to the right, with four bands marked along the number of routers inside the flooding domain. Under 50 routers the cost per topology change is negligible and a single area is fine. Between 50 and 200 routers the cost becomes visible in CPU peaks and flooding bandwidth, so partitioning should start and the core gets its own area. Between 200 and 500 routers the cost is large, and partitioning, summarization and strict control over LSA generation become mandatory. Above 500 routers the design is likely to hit SPF time and memory limits, and the answer is IS-IS with its TLV extensibility, or letting BGP carry the core. A note underneath lists the three things that actually reduce the cost: fewer routers per domain, fewer topology changes, and fewer routers that must recompute.
svg.text: Flooding domain size is a number you choose, and it sets the convergence bill
The cost of one topology change scales with the routers that must hear about it and recompute
routers in the area
cost per
change
< 50 routers · negligible
A single area is perfectly viable. Do not build
hierarchy for a network that does not need it;
hierarchy has its own running cost.
50–200 routers · visible
CPU peaks and LSA flooding bandwidth start
to show. Begin partitioning; give the core its
own area before it is forced on you.
200–500 routers · large
Long SPF runs, slow convergence. Partitioning,
summarization and strict control over which
LSAs get generated are now mandatory.
> 500 routers · at the limit
Likely to hit SPF time and memory limits. Move
to IS-IS for TLV extensibility, or let BGP carry
the core and keep the IGP small.
Three ways to lower the bill, and only three: fewer routers inside the domain (split it), fewer topology changes inside it
(stop the flapping interfaces from being advertised), and fewer routers that must recompute (interface-level timers and throttling).
Adding CPU is not on the list, because the next topology change will be faster than the next hardware refresh.
